q: How do I add reefer (refrigerated container) emissions to my export shipment footprint?
title: Adding reefer emissions to a shipment
short: Calculate the leg as if it were a dry container, then use a reefer-specific factor or apply a reefer uplift for the power the refrigeration unit draws. Add refrigerant leakage only if the carrier reports it, converted to CO2e with a stated GWP. Label any default uplift as an estimate.
audience: Indian exporters of fruit, seafood, dairy and pharmaceuticals

sections.h: Why a reefer emits more than a dry box
p: A reefer container has its own refrigeration unit, powered from the ship's generators at sea, from shore plugs at the terminal, and from a diesel genset on the truck or rail leg. That extra fuel is burnt for your cargo, so a refrigerated shipment carries more emissions per tonne-km than the same weight in a dry container. Frozen cargo at minus 18°C or below usually needs more power than chilled cargo at plus 2 to plus 8°C.

sections.h: Three ways to get the reefer figure, best first
ol: Carrier data: ask the shipping line for a reefer emission figure for your booking or trade lane, and whether it is well-to-wake or tank-to-wake.

Reefer factors: the Clean Cargo methodology, published through Smart Freight Centre, gives separate reefer and dry factors per TEU-km for trade lanes. Use the reefer one, and record whether the factor is tank-to-wake or well-to-wake.

Default uplift: when nothing better exists, multiply the dry container result by a published temperature-controlled default from the GLEC Framework or Clean Cargo that fits your mode. Name its source and label the result an estimate.

p: Reefer units use HFC or HFO refrigerants such as R-134a. Leaks are a separate source in CO2e, because the gas is a greenhouse gas in its own right. Carriers rarely report leakage per shipment; include it only when they do, and state the GWP set, for example R-134a at 1,300 in IPCC AR5 or 1,430 in AR4. Do not invent a leak rate to fill the gap.

sections.h: The legs to cover on land
ul: Factory or pack house to port: a refrigerated truck with a diesel reefer unit. If the transporter bills reefer diesel separately, convert it at 2.68 kg CO2 per litre; otherwise apply a temperature-controlled road uplift.
Pre-cooling and terminal plug-in time: part of the hub emissions under ISO 14083; include it if the terminal or carrier gives a figure.
Which legs sit in your Scope 3 depends on who pays for them under your Incoterm.

example.title: Worked example: 22 t of frozen shrimp, Nhava Sheva to Rotterdam (hypothetical uplift and leak)
lines: Sea leg as dry cargo: 22 t x 11,700 km = 2,57,400 tonne-km; x 0.008 kg CO2e per tonne-km = 2,059.2 kg CO2e
Hypothetical reefer uplift of 1.4 (replace with a carrier or Clean Cargo reefer figure): 2,059.2 x 1.4 = 2,882.9 kg CO2e
Hypothetical carrier report of 0.2 kg R-134a leaked for the voyage: 0.2 x 1,300 (AR5) = 260 kg CO2e
Sea leg total: 2,882.9 + 260 = 3,142.9 kg CO2e, about 3.1 t
example.note: The 0.008 factor is the container ship default in Senseible's logistics calculator, built on GLEC Framework v3.0, and 11,700 km is an approximate Suez routing. The 1.4 uplift and the leak are hypothetical, used only to show the arithmetic.

senseible: Senseible reads freight records, and its logistics calculator applies GLEC-based defaults by mode, distance and weight for the dry leg. It has no reefer uplift or refrigerant leakage figure, so add the reefer share from your carrier's data yourself.
